analysis.one_liner: Bans agreements between employers not to hire or recruit each other's workers.
analysis.headline: The bill to outlaw employer no-poach agreements never got a committee vote, a hearing, or floor action, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for two or more employers — including franchise chains and contractor arrangements — to agree not to solicit or hire each other's employees. These "no-poach" agreements hold wages down by limiting where workers can take their skills. The bill lets workers sue for actual and punitive damages plus attorney's fees, and gives the Federal Trade Commission power to enforce the ban. It was introduced late in the session and died in committee without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose job options and wage bargaining are limited when employers agree not to hire each other's employees. Workers in franchise-heavy industries like fast food, and in staffing-heavy fields like health care and tech services, would gain the right to sue and recover damages. The FTC would gain a clear statutory tool against a practice that suppresses wages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in franchise and staffing-heavy industries

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any entity to enter into, enforce, or threaten to enforce an agreement between two or more employers that prohibits or restricts one from soliciting or hiring the other's employees or former employees.
Explicitly covers agreements made through franchise agreements and contractor-subcontractor agreements, the structures through which no-poach clauses are most common in industries like fast food.
Gives any aggrieved worker a private right of action to recover actual damages, punitive damages as allowed by a court, and attorney's fees.
Gives the Federal Trade Commission authority to enforce the ban as an unfair method of competition, with the same powers it has under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — particularly franchise systems, restaurant chains, and large employers that use no-poach clauses — would face FTC enforcement and damages suits. Businesses that argue such agreements serve legitimate purposes (for example, protecting training investments) would lose the ability to use them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Franchise chains and large employers using no-poach clauses

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a bright-line ban with a private right of action carrying punitive damages, which goes beyond existing antitrust enforcement of no-poach agreements and exposes employers to broad litigation over hiring agreements that may have legitimate business purposes.

It overlaps with existing law: the Federal Trade Commission and courts can already challenge no-poach agreements under antitrust statutes, so the bill adds a new enforcement layer whose costs fall on businesses and, through them, potentially on consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real and large: no-poach agreements limit job mobility and suppress wages, and this bill would give workers both an agency enforcer and a courtroom remedy with attorney's fees, which matters because individual wage losses are usually too small to litigate alone. The costs are litigation exposure and loss of a hiring tool for businesses. The bill was a clean, narrowly aimed statute; the main honest objection is the punitive-damages exposure, not the ban itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to an antitrust subcommittee, and no committee ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on April 26, 2018, joined by three Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Nadler, Cicilline, and Crowley.
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Education and the Workforce, Energy and Commerce, and Judiciary — splitting its jurisdiction at the outset.
On May 22, 2018, the House Judiciary Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
No committee or subcommittee action, hearing, or vote followed, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use no-poach agreements — franchise chains, restaurant groups, and large multi-site employers — kept the practice, and workers gained nothing. The bill's supporters were left with no record vote on the merits.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and the Workforce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled three cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Jerrold Nadler, David Cicilline, and Joseph Crowley
for.role: Cosponsors; Nadler and Cicilline were senior Judiciary Committee members on the antitrust subcommittee

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the antitrust subcommittee on May 22, 2018, and never brought it back for a committee vote or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: Speaker Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three committees simultaneously, splitting jurisdiction, under a rule leaving timing to each committee.

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in the primary committee of referral with no hearing or markup for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; there was no roll-call vote because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: No-poach clauses in franchise agreements, common in fast food, cap the wages and job options of hourly workers by keeping rival employers from bidding for them. The bill bans those clauses outright and makes the companies liable for damages.

industries.industry: Large multi-site employers (health care systems, tech and staffing firms)
industries.note: Employers that informally agree not to recruit each other's staff — a practice documented in health care and tech — would lose the wage-suppression benefit and face FTC enforcement and private suits.
Workers gain mobility and bargaining power, plus a court remedy with attorney's fees that makes individual claims practical to bring.
